To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) we performed a comprehensive, systematic analysis of all heterotrimeric Guanine nucleotide-binding protein (G protein) genes in a large panel of malignant melanoma samples and identified novel somatic mutations in G proteins in 17% (14 out of 80 samples) of the samples, and (ii) our findings indicate that multiple mutated heterotrimeric G proteins may be important for melanoma progression.
somatic mutations in the G protein genes GNG10 and GNZ are frequent in melanoma and may play a role in melanoma progression.
we performed a comprehensive, unbiased mutational analysis of heterotrimerc G proteins in melanomas and found mutations in 7 genes in 17% samples.

the identification of novel mutations in the heterotrimal G proteins, and the role of these proteins in melanoma.
the role of G proteins in the pathogenesis of melanoma and the development of targeted therapies.
the role of heterotrimetric G-protein in melanoma.

heterotrimeric guanidine nucleotide-binding proteins are not mutated in melanoma.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
GNAQ mutations are common in uveal melanoma and blue nevi, but are rare in melanomas of other types.
we have identified somatic, non-coding mutations in G proteins in 17% (13 of 79) of melanoma cases, and that the highest rates of sommatic, non-coding mutation were found in GNAQ, GNG10, and GNAZ.

The main takeaway from our work is that
GNAQ is the most commonly mutated G protein gene in melanoma, and that mutations in GNG10, GNAZ and GNAI2 are also common in melanoma.
the heterotrimer of G proteins is a novel oncogene in melanoma, and that G proteins may be a novel therapeutic target in melanoma.
